claims.text: The multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy has a stable microstructure under the initial equilibrium conditions.
Protective thermally grown oxide scales form on the alloy at elevated temperature.
The integrity of the protective oxide scale varies at heterogeneous phase boundaries.
Mechanical wear disrupts the protective thermally grown oxide layers.
Wear-induced oxide disruption exposes fresh alloy surfaces.
The freshly exposed alloy surfaces are more susceptible to localized corrosion than oxide-covered surfaces.
Localized corrosion undermines surface integrity and reduces the alloy's resistance to wear.
Reciprocal enhancement between oxide removal, corrosion, and wear creates a self-reinforcing degradation cycle.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion produce greater total degradation than the sum of degradation from matched wear-only and corrosion-only exposures.
The wear rate during simultaneous exposure is higher than during matched wear-only exposure.
The corrosion rate during simultaneous exposure is higher than during matched corrosion-only exposure.
The proposed mechanism applies when a continuous protective oxide film can form.
The proposed mechanism requires mechanical stresses sufficient to disrupt the oxide film partially without causing bulk plastic deformation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when the alloy does not form a protective oxide scale or when oxide formation is negligible.
The relevant elevated-temperature range is approximately 500–800 °C.
The magnitude of the degradation-rate increase depends on alloy composition and test conditions.
